newsitem.title: FRANCE: Salman Rushdie urges Europe to stand up to Iran.
newsitem.headline: Salman Rushdie urges Europe to stand up to Iran.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie, under an Iranian death sentence for alleged blasphemy, urged Europeans on Thursday to stand up to Iran and defend their traditional values such as freedom of speech.

"What more does Iran have to do for Europe to decide it has had enough and react?" Rushdie told the French National Assembly's foreign affairs commission in a closely guarded hearing open to the public.

The Indian-born author, who incurred the wrath of the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini with his book "The Satanic Verses", told the commission Tehran views murder as part of the "normal political process" and operates "a terrorist network ready to execute orders handed down from on high".

Blasting past and present Iranian leaders, including president-elect Mohammad Khatami, Rushdie urged Europeans to defend the values of their civilisation such as human rights and freedom of speech and to hit Iran with economic sanctions.

The commission, chaired by former culture minister Jack Lang, invited Rushdie amid signs of deteriorating relations between Iran and Europe following a court ruling in Germany this year that Iranian leaders ordered political killings in Berlin in 1992. Iran denied the accusations.

On Wednesday French authorities declined to comment on the identity of an Iranian student expelled from France and who was described by the Iraqi-backed Iranian National Council of Resistance as an Iranian intelligence agent.
Rushdie has lived under Scotland Yard's protection since 1989 when Iranian clergy said his book was blasphemous and injurious and put a price on his head.
He praised Washington's hard line against Tehran and applauded the new British Labour government's approach.

"Words are no longer enough," said Lang. "If Britain, France and Germany are determined, we'll see progress on liberties. Realpolitik is no longer the most realistic strategy. Firmness in defending principles is the way to impress governments which do not respect weak countries."
Lang said it was important for Iran to realise it was dealing with countries ready to go as far as breaking off ties.

Rushdie also met National Assembly President Laurent Fabius, a former Socialist prime minister, who said in a statement he "saluted a man and a writer...who accepts to risk his life not just to pursue his writing but also to defend the freedom of expression everywhere and for all".
